text.p: Boeing Co said on Friday it has recommended that operators of its popular 737 airplane conduct tests of rudder power control units within 10 days to detect a potential jam.

The aerospace giant said in a statement engineers from Boeing and the National Transportation Safety Board discovered a jam of the secondary slide of the rudder power control unit when subjected to extreme temperatures not normally encountered.
Tests revealed the jam could interfere with the normal operation of the aircraft. Boeing has forwarded its findings and recommendations to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Boeing said the problem, which it referred to as "very unlikely", has never been encountered in more than 69 million flights worldwide. Investigations into crashes of Boeing 737's in Colorado Springs in 1991 and Pittsburgh in 1994 did not reveal any problem with the rudder power control unit, the company said.
About 2,700 Boeing 737's are in service worldwide.
The National Transportation Safety Board said the recommendation by Boeing for operators to do rudder tests on 737 jets was a direct result of information gained during NTSB tests.

"While the NTSB supports Boeing's efforts, we are doing a full analysis of this data to find out how it relates to the Pittsburgh and Colorado Springs accidents," NTSB chairman Jim Hall said in a statement.

Hall said recent tests on 737 rudder components by NTSB's investigative team in Seattle, and last month's series of NTSB recommendations on 737s, pointed out more areas for the FAA to consider in the safe operation of 737s.
Last month, the NTSB recommended design changes in the rudder and "yaw" control systems of the widely used 737 to try to avoid sudden and uncontrolled rolls.

The board recommended the FAA require Boeing to make long-term design changes to preclude a loss of control from a rudder "hard-over" - an extreme rudder shift that can throw a plane into a sharp roll.
It also said the rudder damper should be redesigned to avoid "yaws" -- the movement of the nose from side to side -- so the rudder would not move into an extreme roll-causing position.
Boeing later said the FAA is working on an alert to operators to make the recommendations mandatory.
After the initial test, further tests will be required after every 250 flight hours, or about every 30 days for the average 737, a spokesman told reporters.
The company is working on a modification to the 737 and will send materials and cover the costs of modifying all the 737s in operation, the spokesman said.
Boeing said the costs would not be substantial, but declined to elaborate. The modification will not be needed on the latest generation of 737s, it said.

Should the rudder power control unit, which is like the power steering unit on an automobile, have the jamming problem the airplane could roll to one side and possibly go out of control if the pilot reacts incorrectly or if the plane is close to the ground.
Boeing said that despite the recommendations it is still safe to fly on a 737 and that the move was merely to avoid the possibility of a problem, however remote.
